body: cc @JanTvrdik are you able to do some easy fix in the TypeSpecifier? Thanks.

@JanTvrdik it can be solved (I believe) for the cases 
`$foo > [scalar]` and
`[scalar] < $foo`
without knowing the *value* of the scalar variable.

Both operations are guaranteed to return `false` if `$foo` is `null`.

these all evaluate to false
- `null > -100;`
- `null > 100;`
- `null > 0;`
- `null > "hello";`
- `null > "";`
- `null > [];`

Is this even an issue to solve? `$foo > 1` for `?int` means _implicitly convert null to zero and do comparison_, that is something to be avoided in strictly typed code (and maybe already is in strict rules repo, or should be).

> `$foo > 1` for `?int` means implicitly convert null to zero and do comparison

Not in PHP it doesn't. There's no implicit conversion done by the engine – `null` is always treated as a special value, and the comparisons work/don't work accordingly.

Basically it is, implementation is just a bit more optimized to avoid unnecessary zval conversion.
But I'm not talking about implementation, I'm talking about the representation of the operation: you are passing null to an operation not intended for null (not by implementation but by logic). Comparison operation is only intended for numerics, strings and some special objects like DateTime. Other types should be type errors.

> Other types should be type errors

Counterpoint: no they shouldn't.

If a static analysis tool can figure out that the code will always do something, then it should apply those inferences and carry on. The fewer messages it gives to the end user about properly functioning code, the better. And this code functions properly in PHP.

It's not just PHP either. C#, a language I consider to be type safe and still pretty sane about type rules, allows this same comparison on a possibly null value: http://rextester.com/ROI67945.

>The fewer messages it gives to the end user about properly functioning code, the better.

I disgree. It should report as much relevant messages as possible.

> And this code functions properly in PHP.

Hello PHP 4.
Should I even start with all the checks PHPStan does and PHP allows? Take duplicated keys in arrays for example.
PHPStan is not a language compiler, it's a static analysis tool. Reporting null in place of integer in comparison is exactly what is was built for.

I guess we just fundamentally disagree. Of the developers I work with daily, none would think that `null > 1`. Indeed, one of them created a [ticket that I just fixed](https://github.com/vimeo/psalm/issues/186) that mirrored this one.

Given how many thousands of other more serious problems a good static analysis tool can find in a large codebase, this doesn't rate for me.

Sidenote: Flow and TypeScript (in strict null checks mode) both flag the comparison. But Javascript evaluates `null` comparisons differently, where `null > -1` evaluates to `true` (it's always `false` in PHP.

> Of the developers I work with daily, none would think that null > 1.

I never said that, did I? I said null will be implicitly converted to 0 and then evaluated. It's PHP's behavior, I don't contraditct it.
I just believe it should be reported as an issue in code (thus null being disallowed as operand), if not here on higher level, possibly at least in strict repo.

> I said null will be implicitly converted to 0 and then evaluated

But it's not. If it were, `null > -1` would evaluate to `true`, because `0 > -1` evaluates to `true`. But `null > -1` evaluates to `false` in PHP.

Yeah, well, I was wrong then about converting it to zero, but anyway, I never compare nulls so I don't exactly remember these edge cases. :) But that changes nothing about my thinking about (dis)allowing it as operand, maybe even strengthens my opinion to avoid WTF behavior,

PHPStan should correctly understand any code, even loosely typed. That’s why gathering info about code is decoupled from reporting errors in the code.

Disallowing loose comparisons is then a job for the strict-rules repo.

issue.body:
# Bug report

If a value of type `int|false` passes the "greater than zero" test, then its type should be reduced to `int`. However, the value type is still considered `int|false`.

### Code snippet that reproduces the problem

https://phpstan.org/r/042891ee-6a5e-4139-bd8b-08abd04df0ba

### Expected output

No error

body: Looks like the issue is fixed already.

Looks like there are two bugs now (https://phpstan.org/r/e3880862-83e4-40b8-92ce-420fb16811cb):

1) `$foo` is `int<2, max>|null` inside the condition
2) `int` accepts `int<2, max>|null` :(

Maybe @jlherren could look into this? :)
